findings.excerpt:
lemma tendsto_rpow_atBot_of_base_gt_one (b : ℝ) (hb : 1 < b) :
    Tendsto (b ^ · : ℝ → ℝ) atBot (𝓝 0) := by
findings.problem: The hypothesis `1 < b` restricts the lemma to positive bases, but the limit at `atBot` also exists (and equals 0) for every negative base with `|b| > 1`: for `b < -1` and `x → atBot`, `Real.rpow_def_of_neg` gives `b ^ x = exp (log b * x) * cos (x * π)` with `log b = log |b| > 0`, so the exponential decays to 0 while the cosine factor stays bounded. Equivalently `|b ^ x| ≤ |b| ^ x` by `Real.abs_rpow_le_abs_rpow`, and `|b| ^ x → 0`. The file already handles negative bases wherever the `atTop` limit exists (`tendsto_rpow_atTop_of_base_lt_one`, lines 52–66, treats `-1 < b < 0` via `Real.rpow_def_of_nonpos` and the bounded cosine), so the `atBot` statement is the one base-limit lemma with an unnecessarily narrow base range. The degenerate bases are not affected: `b = 0` and `b = ±1` all violate `1 < |b|`.
findings.proposed_change:
Replace the hypothesis `hb : 1 < b` by `hb : 1 < |b|` (the existing case is recovered since `b < |b|` when `1 < b`), i.e. state

  lemma tendsto_rpow_atBot_of_base_gt_one {b : ℝ} (hb : 1 < |b|) :
      Tendsto (b ^ · : ℝ → ℝ) atBot (𝓝 0)

Proof sketch: apply the positive-base case to `|b|` to get `Tendsto (fun x => |b| ^ x) atBot (𝓝 0)`; by `Real.abs_rpow_le_abs_rpow b x` and `Real.rpow_nonneg (abs_nonneg b) x` we have `0 ≤ |b ^ x| ≤ |b| ^ x` for all `x`, so `squeeze_zero` gives `Tendsto (fun x => |b ^ x|) atBot (𝓝 0)`, which is equivalent to `Tendsto (fun x => b ^ x) atBot (𝓝 0)`. Keeping the positive-base case as a separate (private) lemma avoids any circularity.
findings.benefit: The four lemmas about limits of `b ^ ·` at `±∞` would then cover exactly the base ranges for which a limit exists (`|b| < 1` at `atTop`, `|b| > 1` at `atBot`, positive base `< 1` at `atBot`), giving a reader a uniform picture instead of silently dropping the negative-base `atBot` case. Users with negative bases (e.g. recurrences or products involving `(-c) ^ x`) can apply the lemma directly rather than re-deriving the cosine/absolute-value argument used in `tendsto_rpow_atTop_of_base_lt_one`.

findings.excerpt: lemma tendsto_log_mul_self_nhdsLT_zero : Filter.Tendsto (fun x ↦ log x * x) (𝓝[<] 0) (𝓝 0) := by
findings.problem: The left one-sided limit is stated only for the fixed exponent `1` (`log x * x`), although the same limit holds for every positive real exponent `r`, exactly as in the right-hand companion `tendsto_log_mul_rpow_nhdsGT_zero` (lines 398–401). For `x < 0`, `Real.rpow_def_of_neg` gives `x ^ r = exp (log x * r) * cos (r * π)` and `log x = log (-x)`, hence `log x * x ^ r = cos (r * π) * (log (-x) * (-x) ^ r)`, and the right-hand limit applies to `-x → 0⁺`. The current proof carries out precisely this kind of reduction (via `abs`, `log_abs`, `tendsto_abs_nhdsNE_zero`) for the single exponent 1, so the special case is not cheaper than the general one. The degenerate case `cos (π * r) = 0` is harmless: then `x ^ r = 0` for `x < 0` and the product is identically `0`.
findings.proposed_change:
State the general version first

  lemma tendsto_log_mul_rpow_nhdsLT_zero {r : ℝ} (hr : 0 < r) :
      Tendsto (fun x ↦ log x * x ^ r) (𝓝[<] 0) (𝓝 0)

and keep the current lemma as a one-line corollary `simpa only [Real.rpow_one] using tendsto_log_mul_rpow_nhdsLT_zero one_pos`. Proof of the general version: on `Iio 0`, rewrite with `Real.rpow_def_of_neg hx`, `Real.log_neg_eq_log` and `Real.rpow_def_of_pos (neg_pos.mpr hx)` to get `log x * x ^ r = cos (π * r) * (log (-x) * (-x) ^ r)`; compose `tendsto_log_mul_rpow_nhdsGT_zero hr` with `Tendsto (fun x : ℝ => -x) (𝓝[<] 0) (𝓝[>] 0)` and multiply by the constant `cos (π * r)`.
findings.benefit: The file's `x → 0⁻` results would no longer be a lone exponent-1 case: users needing `x ^ r * log x → 0` from the left (e.g. one-sided continuity or integrability of `x ↦ x ^ r * log x` near 0) get the statement for all `r > 0` without redoing the negative-base/absolute-value reduction. The existing uses in `NegMulLog.lean`/`InvLog.lean` continue to work through the derived `r = 1` corollary, so nothing is obscured.
